words.shortDefinition: An online storefront offering thousands of prebuilt VM images, applications, and services from Microsoft and third-party vendors, ready to deploy in one click.
words.simpleDefinition: It is a storefront inside Azure where you can find and deploy prebuilt software solutions — databases, security tools, developer environments, and more — without building them from scratch. Vendors publish certified images and managed apps, and you pay through your Azure bill. It saves teams from hunting for and vetting software separately.
words.longDefinition: Azure Marketplace is a curated catalog of thousands of commercial and open-source applications, virtual machine images, container images, consulting services, and developer tools published by Microsoft and independent software vendors (ISVs). Resources deploy directly into a customer's subscription via Azure Resource Manager, keeping procurement, billing, and governance unified. Offerings span categories including AI/ML, security, networking, databases, and DevOps; many are certified by Microsoft for compatibility and security. Some listings include free trials or BYOL (bring your own license) options, while others integrate transactional billing directly into Azure invoices for simplified procurement. Organizations with Private Marketplace can curate which offers are visible to their teams.
words.connector: Like an app store for cloud infrastructure: instead of building every tool yourself, you pick tested, vendor-certified solutions off the shelf and deploy them directly.
words.techContext: The security team found a certified WAF appliance in Azure Marketplace and deployed it into the hub VNet in under ten minutes.
words.exampleSentence: Instead of manually configuring Redis, we pulled the pre-hardened image straight from Azure Marketplace and had it running in minutes.

codeExample.code:
# Find Marketplace VM images for a publisher
az vm image list --publisher Bitnami --offer wordpress --all --output table

words.etymology: From 'marketplace' (a venue for buying and selling), prefixed with the Azure brand name.

words.shortDefinition: A geographic area containing one or more data centers grouped to provide low-latency compute and storage, forming the primary deployment boundary for most Azure resources.
words.simpleDefinition: An Azure Region is a specific geographic location — like East US or West Europe — where Microsoft operates clusters of data centers. When you deploy a resource you pick a Region, and your data stays there by default. Picking the right Region affects latency for your users and which compliance rules apply.
words.longDefinition: An Azure Region is a set of data centers, deployed within a latency-defined perimeter and connected through a dedicated low-latency network, that Azure uses to deliver services. As of 2026 Azure spans over 60 regions worldwide, making it one of the largest global footprints of any cloud provider. Most Azure resources are region-scoped, meaning they exist in and are billed to a specific region; data residency and compliance boundaries align to regions. Each region pairs with another for geo-redundant backups and failover via Azure-managed paired regions. Not all services or SKUs are available in every region, and pricing can vary by geography.
words.connector: Like a city's post-office district: your mail (data) stays in your assigned city unless you explicitly forward it elsewhere.
words.techContext: The team deployed the production workload to the North Europe region to satisfy GDPR data-residency requirements for their EU customers.
words.exampleSentence: We chose the Australia East region so that end-users in Sydney experience single-digit-millisecond latency to our APIs.

codeExample.code:
# List all available Azure regions
az account list-locations --output table

words.etymology: From the Latin 'regio' (territory, district), used here to denote a geographic deployment boundary.

words.shortDefinition: An independent data center, or cluster of data centers, within a single Region that has separate power, cooling, and networking to protect workloads from facility-level failures.
words.simpleDefinition: Availability Zones are like separate buildings within the same city: close enough for low latency, but far enough apart that a power outage in one won't affect the others. Spreading VMs or databases across zones means your service survives a zone-level failure. They are the building block of high-availability designs in Azure.
words.longDefinition: Azure Availability Zones are physically separate locations within an Azure Region, each consisting of one or more data centers with independent power supplies, cooling systems, and networking. They are connected by a high-bandwidth, low-latency private fiber network (typically sub-2 ms intra-region), enabling synchronous replication for zone-redundant storage accounts, databases, and load-balanced VM sets. A region that supports zones has at least three, numbered Zone 1, 2, and 3. Services like Azure Virtual Machines, Azure Kubernetes Service, and Azure SQL Database offer zone-redundant or zone-pinned SKUs. Unlike Availability Sets (which protect against rack-level failures in a single data center), Availability Zones protect against entire facility outages and support Azure's 99.99% VM SLA.
words.connector: Like having offices in three separate skyscrapers downtown: a fire in one building doesn't shut down the other two, and staff can reach any building quickly.
words.techContext: By deploying the application tier across three availability zones and using a zone-redundant load balancer, the team achieved a 99.99% uptime SLA.
words.exampleSentence: After the cooling failure knocked out Zone 2, traffic shifted seamlessly to the VMs running in Zones 1 and 3.

codeExample.code:
# Create a VM pinned to availability zone 1
az vm create --resource-group prod-rg --name web-vm-z1 \
  --image Ubuntu2204 --zone 1 --size Standard_D2s_v5

words.etymology: From 'availability' (the ability to be accessed) + 'zone' (a delineated area); analogous to AWS Availability Zones.

words.shortDefinition: A logical container for related Azure resources that share a common lifecycle, enabling collective management, deployment, and deletion.
words.simpleDefinition: A resource group bundles Azure resources — virtual machines, databases, storage accounts — that belong together so you can manage, tag, and delete them as a single unit. Every Azure resource must live in exactly one resource group. Teams typically create one per environment (dev, staging, prod) or per application.
words.longDefinition: An Azure Resource Group is a metadata container that holds references to resources deployed in a subscription; the resources themselves run in a region but the resource group can technically span regions (though the metadata is stored in the resource group's own location). It acts as the primary scope for RBAC assignments, policy application, cost management via Azure Cost Management, and ARM template deployments. Deleting a resource group deletes all resources inside it, making it powerful for lifecycle management (e.g., teardown of a dev environment). A resource can only belong to one resource group, but it can interact with resources in other groups. Resource groups are free — there is no charge for the container itself.
words.connector: Like a labeled project folder on your desk: everything for one project goes in the folder, and throwing out the folder cleans up everything at once.
words.techContext: The CI/CD pipeline creates a resource group per pull request, deploys a test environment into it, runs integration tests, then deletes the group to avoid lingering costs.
words.exampleSentence: When the project ended, we deleted the resource group and every VM, disk, and database inside it was gone in one command.

codeExample.code:
# Create a resource group, then delete it (and all contents)
az group create --name my-app-rg --location eastus
az group delete --name my-app-rg --yes --no-wait

words.etymology: From 'resource' (a cloud asset) + 'group' (a collection); a core organizing concept introduced with Azure Resource Manager.

words.shortDefinition: The unified control plane for deploying, updating, and managing all Azure resources, enforcing consistent access control and tagging across every operation.
words.simpleDefinition: It is the layer that sits between you and Azure's backend services, handling every create, read, update, and delete request for resources. Whether you use the portal, CLI, PowerShell, or an ARM template, every call goes through it. It ensures consistent authentication, authorization, and policy enforcement.
words.longDefinition: Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the deployment and management service that forms Azure's control plane. All interactions with Azure resources — from the Portal, Azure CLI, PowerShell, REST API, or SDKs — are routed through ARM, which authenticates the caller via Microsoft Entra ID, checks RBAC permissions, evaluates Azure Policy, and applies locks before forwarding the request to the appropriate resource provider (e.g., Microsoft.Compute, Microsoft.Storage). ARM enables declarative infrastructure-as-code via ARM templates (JSON) and Bicep, which it transpiles and evaluates in dependency order. It supports resource groups, tags, cross-resource dependency tracking during deployment, and roll-back on failure. Everything you deploy in Azure is managed through ARM, making it the authoritative source of resource state.
words.connector: Like a city's building-permit office: every construction project must submit plans through it, which checks zoning rules, issues approvals, and logs what was built where.
words.techContext: All infrastructure changes go through ARM, which means RBAC denials and policy violations are caught uniformly regardless of whether the engineer uses the CLI or the Portal.
words.exampleSentence: Because every tool routes through Azure Resource Manager, the same RBAC role that blocks a portal action also blocks an equivalent CLI command.

codeExample.code:
# Deploy resources declaratively via ARM (using az deployment group)
az deployment group create \
  --resource-group prod-rg \
  --template-file main.bicep \
  --parameters @prod.parameters.json

words.etymology: 'Resource Manager' is a descriptive name; the ARM control plane replaced the older Azure Service Management (ASM/Classic) model in 2014.

words.shortDefinition: A billing and access boundary that groups Azure resource consumption under a single account, with its own spending limits and access-control policies.
words.simpleDefinition: A subscription is like an account with Azure: resources you create are billed to it and governed by its policies. Large organizations use multiple subscriptions to isolate teams, environments, or regions. Every resource group and resource belongs to exactly one subscription.
words.longDefinition: An Azure subscription is a logical unit that provides authenticated and authorized access to Azure products and services, and is the primary billing boundary — usage is invoiced per subscription. Each subscription is associated with a single Azure tenant (Microsoft Entra ID directory) but a tenant can have many subscriptions. Quotas and service limits are per-subscription, and many compliance or isolation requirements are enforced at this boundary. Subscriptions sit below management groups and above resource groups in the hierarchy. Common patterns include having separate subscriptions for production, non-production, and shared services, or per-business-unit subscriptions in a landing-zone design. Spending limits (only for trial subscriptions) and cost budgets can be applied at the subscription level.
words.connector: Like a corporate credit card for a department: all purchases go on it, the finance team sees spending, and IT can set the card's usage rules.
words.techContext: The platform team provisions a new Azure subscription for each product team, keeping blast radius, billing, and RBAC boundaries cleanly separated.
words.exampleSentence: We moved the production workload to its own subscription so a misconfiguration in the dev subscription could never affect production resources.

codeExample.code:
# List all subscriptions accessible to the logged-in account
az account list --output table
# Switch to a specific subscription
az account set --subscription "My Prod Subscription"

words.etymology: From 'subscription' (an agreement to receive a service), adapted to the cloud billing model.

words.shortDefinition: A container sitting above subscriptions in the Azure hierarchy, used to apply governance policies and RBAC across many subscriptions at once.
words.simpleDefinition: Management groups let you organize subscriptions into a tree, then apply policies and role assignments once at a high level and have them cascade down. Without them, you would have to apply the same policy to every subscription individually. They are essential once an organization has dozens of subscriptions.
words.longDefinition: Azure Management Groups provide a hierarchical governance scope above subscriptions. An organization starts with a root management group (tenant root) and can nest up to six levels of child management groups beneath it. Azure Policy assignments and RBAC role assignments made at a management group scope are inherited by all subscriptions and resources beneath that node, enabling consistent enforcement of security baselines, allowed regions, required tags, or naming conventions across an entire organization without per-subscription repetition. Management groups align to Control Tower's OUs conceptually and are the foundation of Azure Landing Zones and the Cloud Adoption Framework governance model. Each tenant can have up to 10,000 management groups, and moving a subscription between groups immediately applies the target group's policies.
words.connector: Like a company org chart where rules set at the division level automatically apply to every department beneath it, saving you from repeating the same directive to each team.
words.techContext: The CISO assigns the 'no public IP on storage accounts' policy at the Corp management group so it cascades to all 40 subscriptions automatically.
words.exampleSentence: Adding the new EU subscription under the 'GDPR' management group instantly applied all the required data-residency policies without manual steps.

codeExample.code:
# Create a management group and move a subscription into it
az account management-group create --name corp-gdpr --display-name "GDPR Workloads"
az account management-group subscription add \
  --name corp-gdpr --subscription <subscriptionId>

words.etymology: Descriptive: a 'group' at the 'management' level of the Azure hierarchy, introduced in 2018.

words.shortDefinition: Microsoft's cloud-based identity and access management directory that authenticates users and authorizes access to Azure and thousands of other applications.
words.simpleDefinition: Formerly called Azure Active Directory, it is the identity backbone for Azure and Microsoft 365. It manages user accounts, groups, multi-factor authentication, and single sign-on to cloud and on-premises apps. Every Azure subscription trusts exactly one Entra ID tenant.
words.longDefinition: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) is Microsoft's cloud-native identity platform, functioning as a multi-tenant, cloud-based directory and identity management service. It handles authentication (via OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, SAML 2.0, and WS-Federation), authorization, MFA, conditional access policies, passwordless authentication (FIDO2/Hello), and B2B/B2C identity scenarios. Entra ID integrates with thousands of SaaS applications via the app gallery, and supports hybrid identity by syncing with on-premises Active Directory Domain Services via Microsoft Entra Connect. Every Azure subscription is associated with one Entra ID tenant, making it the authentication authority for all Azure RBAC and ARM operations. Security features include identity protection (risk-based sign-in policies), Privileged Identity Management (just-in-time role elevation), and access reviews.
words.connector: Like a company's HR and security-badge system combined: it knows who you are, what you're allowed to enter, and can add or revoke access instantly.
words.techContext: The application registers a service principal in Microsoft Entra ID and uses the client-credentials flow to obtain tokens for calling the Azure REST API.
words.exampleSentence: After enabling Conditional Access in Microsoft Entra ID, logins from unmanaged devices are automatically blocked unless the user completes MFA.

codeExample.code:
# Create a user in Microsoft Entra ID
az ad user create \
  --display-name "Dev Bot" \
  --user-principal-name devbot@contoso.onmicrosoft.com \
  --password 'P@ssw0rd123!'

words.etymology: 'Entra' derives from the Latin 'intrare' (to enter/access); rebranded from Azure Active Directory in 2023.

words.shortDefinition: A cross-platform command-line tool that lets engineers create, manage, and automate Azure resources using the `az` command from any terminal.
words.simpleDefinition: The Azure CLI is the `az` command you run in your terminal to interact with Azure from any operating system. It wraps the Azure REST API in human-friendly commands and is great for scripting, automation, and quick one-off operations. It is the go-to tool for engineers who prefer the command line over clicking through a web console.
words.longDefinition: The Azure CLI (Command-Line Interface) is an open-source, cross-platform tool written in Python that provides a consistent command experience for managing Azure resources on Windows, macOS, Linux, and Azure Cloud Shell. All commands follow the pattern `az <group> <subcommand> [options]` and communicate with Azure via its REST API using your authenticated session (interactive browser login, service principal, or managed identity). Output formats include JSON (default), table, YAML, and TSv. It supports JMESPath queries for filtering output, `--no-wait` for fire-and-forget operations, and `az interactive` for autocomplete. The Azure CLI is versioned independently of Azure services and is updated frequently; `az upgrade` refreshes it in place. For automation, it pairs naturally with Bash scripts, CI/CD pipelines, and GitHub Actions.
words.connector: Like a TV remote for Azure: instead of walking to the TV (the portal) and pushing buttons by hand, you issue precise commands from your couch (terminal) instantly.
words.techContext: The deployment pipeline calls `az acr build` and `az containerapp update` in sequence, pushing a new image and rolling it out without touching the portal.
words.exampleSentence: She scripted the entire staging environment teardown in a Bash file using the Azure CLI so any teammate could reproduce it in minutes.

codeExample.code:
# Log in and show the current account context
az login
az account show --output table

words.etymology: CLI = Command-Line Interface; 'Azure CLI' simply names the command-line interface for Azure.

words.shortDefinition: A web-based graphical console at portal.azure.com for creating, configuring, monitoring, and managing Azure resources through a browser.
words.simpleDefinition: The Azure Portal is the website where you click through to create VMs, configure databases, set up networking, and view dashboards — no command line required. It is the visual control center for Azure and is often the first place engineers explore when learning the platform. It supports customizable dashboards and pinned resources.
words.longDefinition: The Azure Portal (portal.azure.com) is a web-based, unified management console built as a single-page application running in any modern browser. It provides a graphical interface to Azure Resource Manager, exposing service blades for every Azure product — from creating a VM or App Service to configuring network security groups, reviewing diagnostics, and browsing cost breakdowns. The portal includes a built-in Cloud Shell terminal, a universal search bar for finding resources and docs, pinnable dashboard tiles for monitoring KPIs, and guided deployment wizards that generate ARM/Bicep templates at the end. Access is controlled by the same Microsoft Entra ID authentication and RBAC as all other ARM paths, so the portal is not a privileged backdoor — it obeys the same role assignments as the CLI. It supports multiple language localizations and high-contrast accessibility modes.
words.connector: Like a bank's website: all your accounts and transactions in one place, with a friendly interface for everyday tasks — even if power users prefer the phone-banking CLI.
words.techContext: The on-call engineer used the portal's metrics blade to correlate a spike in 5xx errors with a storage account throttling event, then opened a support ticket in the same window.
words.exampleSentence: New team members learn Azure by exploring in the portal first, then move to the CLI once they understand what each resource is for.

codeExample.code:
# Open the Azure Portal in the default browser (macOS)
open https://portal.azure.com

words.etymology: From 'portal' (a gateway or entry point), reflecting its role as the main browser-based entry into Azure.

words.shortDefinition: A JSON file that declaratively describes the desired state of Azure resources, enabling repeatable and consistent infrastructure deployments.
words.simpleDefinition: An ARM template is a JSON file you hand to Azure that says exactly what resources you want — VMs, storage, networks — and Azure creates or updates them to match. Because it is declarative, deploying the same template twice is safe (idempotent). Bicep is a cleaner language that compiles down to this same format.
words.longDefinition: Azure Resource Manager templates are JSON documents that declare the desired state of Azure infrastructure: resources and their properties, parameters for customization, variables, outputs, and `dependsOn` relationships that control deployment order. ARM evaluates the template against the current resource state and makes only the changes needed to reach the declared state, making deployments idempotent. Templates can be nested or linked for modular design. They are deployed via the CLI (`az deployment group create`), PowerShell, the portal, or a pipeline. Because Bicep — a domain-specific language with cleaner syntax — transpiles to ARM JSON, ARM templates are effectively the compilation target for Azure IaC. ARM templates integrate with Azure Deployment Stacks for lifecycle management and Policy for guardrail enforcement at deploy time.
words.connector: Like a blueprint for a building: the architect draws what the finished structure should look like, and the construction crew builds exactly that, no matter how many times you run it.
words.techContext: The platform team stores ARM templates in a Git repo; a GitHub Actions workflow runs `az deployment sub create` on every merge to main, ensuring drift-free infrastructure.
words.exampleSentence: Because the ARM template is idempotent, re-deploying after a failed run picks up exactly where it left off without duplicating resources.
words.etymology: ARM = Azure Resource Manager; 'template' from Latin 'templum' (a pattern or mold).

words.shortDefinition: A browser-based, authenticated terminal embedded in the Azure Portal that provides a persistent shell environment with Azure CLI, PowerShell, and common developer tools preinstalled.
words.simpleDefinition: Cloud Shell is a terminal that runs inside your browser, already logged into your Azure account, with the Azure CLI and PowerShell ready to use. No local installation is needed. Your files persist in an Azure Storage account between sessions so you can keep scripts there.
words.longDefinition: Azure Cloud Shell is a managed, interactive shell environment accessible from the Azure Portal, the Azure mobile app, and shell.azure.com. It offers both Bash (with Azure CLI, kubectl, Helm, Terraform, Ansible, and common Linux tools) and PowerShell (with the Az module) sessions, running in a containerized environment on Microsoft-managed infrastructure. On first launch it provisions a small Azure Storage file share (in a resource group prefixed `cloud-shell-storage`) to persist your $HOME across sessions. Authentication is automatic via your portal session, so there is no need to run `az login`. It is especially useful for demos, quick one-off scripts, or environments where installing tools locally is restricted. Session idle timeout is 20 minutes.
words.connector: Like a company-issued laptop that's always pre-configured and logged in, accessible from any computer with a browser — no setup, no forgotten passwords.
words.techContext: During a live incident the on-call engineer opened Cloud Shell from their phone's browser and ran kubectl commands against the AKS cluster without needing a VPN client.
words.exampleSentence: Instead of asking the new hire to install the Azure CLI locally, the team lead pointed them to Cloud Shell and they were running commands within seconds.

codeExample.code:
# Cloud Shell auto-authenticates; verify and list resource groups
az account show
az group list --output table

words.etymology: 'Cloud' (internet-hosted) + 'Shell' (a command-line interpreter environment); launched as a feature of the portal in 2017.

words.shortDefinition: An on-demand, configurable compute instance running Linux or Windows on Azure's infrastructure, giving full OS-level control over the environment.
words.simpleDefinition: An Azure Virtual Machine is a server you rent in the cloud. You choose the size (CPU, RAM), the operating system, and the region, then Azure boots it in minutes. You get full admin access — unlike a PaaS service, you are responsible for patching and configuring the OS.
words.longDefinition: Azure Virtual Machines (VMs) are Infrastructure-as-a-Service compute resources that emulate physical servers on Azure's hypervisor infrastructure (Hyper-V based). Each VM is defined by a series: D-series for general purpose, E-series for memory-optimized, N-series for GPU workloads, and specialized HPC series, among others. Storage is provided via managed disks (OS disk + optional data disks). VMs integrate with Virtual Networks for private networking, Azure Load Balancer or Application Gateway for traffic distribution, and Availability Sets or Zones for high availability. Billing is per-second for compute (plus storage and networking); Reserved Instances and Spot VMs provide significant discounts for committed or fault-tolerant workloads. Azure VM extensions and cloud-init enable post-deployment configuration. The Azure Hybrid Benefit reduces costs for customers with existing Windows Server or SQL Server licenses.
words.connector: Like renting a fully furnished server room in someone else's building: you control what runs inside, but the landlord owns the hardware and keeps the lights on.
words.techContext: The legacy monolith runs on a D16s_v5 Azure Virtual Machine with a 1 TB Premium SSD data disk, behind an internal load balancer.
words.exampleSentence: The team created an Azure Virtual Machine with Ubuntu 22.04, installed the app, and snapshotted it as a custom image for the auto-scaling group.

codeExample.code:
# Create a simple Ubuntu VM with a public IP
az vm create \
  --resource-group dev-rg \
  --name my-ubuntu-vm \
  --image Ubuntu2204 \
  --admin-username azureuser \
  --generate-ssh-keys

words.etymology: 'Virtual machine' is a decades-old computing concept (from IBM VM/370, 1972); Azure is Microsoft's cloud brand.

words.shortDefinition: A fully managed platform for hosting web applications, REST APIs, and mobile backends in multiple languages without provisioning or managing underlying servers.
words.simpleDefinition: App Service lets you deploy your web app or API by pushing code or a container — Azure handles the OS, runtime patching, scaling, and load balancing for you. It supports many languages (Node.js, Python, .NET, Java, PHP, Ruby) and can auto-scale on HTTP traffic. You pay for the compute tier, not per request.
words.longDefinition: Azure App Service is a Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) offering that hosts web applications, RESTful APIs, and WebJobs (background tasks) on managed, multi-tenant infrastructure. Developers deploy via Git/GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, ZIP upload, or container registries; the platform handles OS updates, scaling, SSL termination, and load balancing. App Service Plans define the underlying compute tier (Free, Shared, Basic, Standard, Premium, Isolated), with Standard and above supporting autoscale rules based on CPU, memory, or HTTP queue depth. Built-in features include deployment slots for staged rollouts (swap staging → production with near-zero downtime), custom domains with managed TLS certificates via ACM, VNet integration for private backend connectivity, authentication/authorization via Easy Auth (Entra ID, social providers), and application insights for telemetry. The Isolated tier (App Service Environment) deploys into a customer's VNet for network isolation at scale.
words.connector: Like renting a catered office suite instead of building a building: you focus on your work, and the building's management handles elevators, utilities, and maintenance.
words.techContext: The product API runs on an App Service Premium P2v3 plan with five deployment slots — one per feature branch — enabling parallel testing before a staging-to-production slot swap.
words.exampleSentence: The startup deployed their Django API to Azure App Service in an afternoon without touching a server, Nginx config, or SSL certificate.

codeExample.code:
# Create an App Service plan and deploy a Node.js web app
az appservice plan create --name my-plan --resource-group dev-rg \
  --sku B1 --is-linux
az webapp create --resource-group dev-rg --plan my-plan \
  --name my-node-app --runtime 'NODE:20-lts'

words.etymology: 'App Service' is a descriptive Microsoft brand name for a managed application-hosting service, launched in 2014.

words.shortDefinition: The top-level Azure namespace that acts as a unique, billable container for all Azure storage services including blobs, files, queues, and tables.
words.simpleDefinition: A storage account is the entry point for Azure storage: you create one and it gives you a unique URL namespace and access keys for storing blobs, files, queues, and table data. One account can hold petabytes across all four storage types. You choose redundancy, performance tier, and access controls when creating it.
words.longDefinition: An Azure Storage Account is the foundational resource that groups Azure's storage services — Blob Storage, Azure Files, Queue Storage, and Table Storage — under a single namespace with a globally unique account name (e.g., `mystorageaccount.blob.core.windows.net`). Account-level settings control redundancy (LRS, ZRS, GRS, GZRS), performance tier (Standard HDD-backed or Premium SSD-backed), access tier defaults (Hot, Cool, Cold, Archive for blobs), public or private network access, and authorization methods (shared key, SAS tokens, or Microsoft Entra ID). Storage accounts are billed per GB stored, per operation, and for data egress. Multiple redundancy options provide durability across racks (LRS), zones (ZRS), or regions (GRS/GZRS). Hierarchical Namespace can be enabled to make Blob Storage behave as an ADLS Gen2 data lake for analytics workloads.
words.connector: Like a bank account that holds different savings products (checking, certificates, savings bonds) under one account number with shared access controls.
words.techContext: The data pipeline writes raw event JSON to one storage account's blob container, while a separate account with hierarchical namespace enabled serves as the Parquet-formatted ADLS Gen2 data lake.
words.exampleSentence: Because all four blob containers, the file share, and the backup queue share one storage account, access policies and billing roll up in a single place.

codeExample.code:
# Create a general-purpose v2 storage account with ZRS redundancy
az storage account create \
  --name mystorageacct01 \
  --resource-group prod-rg \
  --location eastus \
  --sku Standard_ZRS \
  --kind StorageV2

words.etymology: From 'storage' (the act of storing data) + 'account' (a record or grouping unit in a billing system).

words.shortDefinition: Azure's massively scalable object-storage service for unstructured data — files, images, logs, backups, and media — accessible via HTTPS and REST.
words.simpleDefinition: Blob Storage is where you put files that don't fit neatly into a database: images, videos, log archives, backups, and flat-file datasets. You organize them in containers (like folders) inside a storage account and access them over HTTPS. It scales to exabytes automatically.
words.longDefinition: Azure Blob Storage is an object-storage service designed for massive scale of unstructured data, organized into storage accounts → containers → blobs. Blob types are Block Blob (general files, up to ~190 TB, optimized for sequential access), Append Blob (write-only append for logging), and Page Blob (random-read/write, used for VM disk backing). Access tiers — Hot (frequent access), Cool (infrequent), Cold, and Archive (rare; rehydration required) — let you balance cost and latency at the blob or container level with lifecycle management policies automating transitions. Blob Storage integrates with Azure CDN for global delivery, Azure Data Factory and Synapse for analytics, and Microsoft Entra ID / SAS tokens / access policies for fine-grained authorization. The ADLS Gen2 feature (hierarchical namespace) adds POSIX-style directory semantics for big-data analytics scenarios. Redundancy mirrors the parent storage account's setting.
words.connector: Like an unlimited warehouse for any physical item: shelves hold anything regardless of shape, you address each box by name, and climate control (access tier) trades cost for retrieval speed.
words.techContext: Nightly database exports are compressed and streamed into a Cool-tier blob container, with a lifecycle rule that moves objects older than 90 days to Archive tier.
words.exampleSentence: The media platform stores 50 TB of user-uploaded videos in blob containers and serves them through Azure CDN using SAS token URLs.

codeExample.code:
# Upload a file and generate a 1-hour read SAS URL
az storage blob upload --account-name mystorageacct01 \
  --container-name uploads --name report.csv --file ./report.csv
az storage blob generate-sas --account-name mystorageacct01 \
  --container-name uploads --name report.csv \
  --permissions r --expiry 2026-06-14T02:00:00Z --https-only

words.etymology: BLOB = Binary Large OBject, a term from database systems; 'storage' denotes the cloud service category.

words.shortDefinition: A virtual hard disk in Azure that is fully managed as a durable, high-availability block-storage volume attached to virtual machines, with no storage account management required.
words.simpleDefinition: A managed disk is a virtual hard drive for Azure VMs where Microsoft handles all the underlying storage account management, replication, and hardware for you. You create one, specify the size and performance tier, and attach it to a VM. Snapshots, encryption at rest with customer-managed keys, and zone-redundancy are all built in.
words.longDefinition: Azure Managed Disks are block-storage volumes for Azure Virtual Machines, designed to replace the earlier unmanaged-disk model (which required customers to manage storage accounts and VHD blobs). Each managed disk is an isolated resource with its own ARM ID, supports RBAC, and is backed by Azure Storage, providing durability and 99.999% availability. Disk types include Ultra Disk (sub-millisecond latency, configurable IOPS/throughput), Premium SSD v2 (high performance with flexible sizing), Premium SSD, Standard SSD, and Standard HDD, enabling cost-performance tradeoffs across workloads. Managed disks support server-side encryption by default using platform-managed keys, with the option for customer-managed keys via Azure Key Vault. Incremental snapshots enable cost-efficient backups (only changed blocks are stored). Shared disks allow simultaneous attachment to multiple VMs for clustered scenarios.
words.connector: Like a USB drive that Azure stores and manages in a secure vault: you plug it into whichever VM needs it, and Azure handles durability and redundancy behind the scenes.
words.techContext: The database VM uses a 4 TB Premium SSD v2 managed disk configured for 10,000 IOPS and 400 MB/s throughput, sized independently of storage capacity.
words.exampleSentence: After the VM failure, the engineer detached the managed disk, attached it to a recovery VM, and retrieved the data without any data loss.

codeExample.code:
# Create a 256 GB Premium SSD managed disk
az disk create \
  --resource-group prod-rg \
  --name app-data-disk \
  --size-gb 256 \
  --sku Premium_LRS \
  --zone 1

words.etymology: 'Managed' indicates Microsoft manages the underlying infrastructure; 'disk' is computing shorthand for a block-storage volume.

words.shortDefinition: A logically isolated private network in Azure that lets resources communicate securely, with full control over IP addressing, subnets, routing, and connectivity.
words.simpleDefinition: A Virtual Network (VNet) is your private network in the cloud: you define an IP address space, carve it into subnets, and Azure resources you place inside communicate privately. Traffic stays within Azure's backbone unless you explicitly add internet or hybrid connectivity. It is the foundation of every Azure network architecture.
words.longDefinition: An Azure Virtual Network (VNet) is the fundamental networking primitive that provides isolation, segmentation, and controlled connectivity for Azure resources. Each VNet has one or more CIDR address spaces and is divided into subnets that can be associated with Network Security Groups and route tables. Resources in the same VNet communicate over private IPs by default; connectivity to other VNets is achieved via VNet Peering or VPN Gateway. Internet-inbound traffic requires a public IP on a resource or a load balancer; internet-egress travels through Azure's backbone to the internet, optionally via NAT Gateway for fixed outbound IPs. VNets integrate with private endpoints, service endpoints, Azure Firewall, Application Gateway, and on-premises networks via VPN Gateway or ExpressRoute. VNets are free; charges apply to components like gateways, NAT, and peering data transfer.
words.connector: Like wiring your own private LAN in a leased data center: you define the network topology, and the landlord's routers enforce the walls between your network and everyone else's.
words.techContext: All compute resources deploy into a hub-and-spoke VNet architecture: a shared-services hub VNet with peering connections to spoke VNets for each business unit.
words.exampleSentence: By placing the database server and web app in the same Virtual Network with no public IP on the DB, the team ensured database traffic never touches the internet.

codeExample.code:
# Create a VNet with a 10.0.0.0/16 address space
az network vnet create \
  --resource-group prod-rg \
  --name prod-vnet \
  --address-prefix 10.0.0.0/16 \
  --location eastus

words.etymology: 'Virtual' (software-defined) + 'network' (interconnected computing devices); the concept mirrors on-premises LAN/WAN in cloud form.

words.shortDefinition: A stateful firewall resource containing inbound and outbound rules that control traffic to subnets and individual network interfaces based on ports, protocols, and IP ranges.
words.simpleDefinition: An NSG is a list of allow/deny rules that act as a firewall for traffic flowing to and from Azure resources. You associate it with a subnet or a VM's network card, and Azure evaluates rules in priority order. Lower priority numbers win, and there is an implicit deny-all at the end of every list.
words.longDefinition: An Azure Network Security Group (NSG) is a stateful packet-filtering resource containing ordered inbound and outbound security rules, each specifying a priority (100–4096, lower wins), protocol (TCP/UDP/ICMP/Any), source and destination (IP, CIDR, service tag, or application security group), port range, and action (Allow/Deny). NSGs can be associated with subnets (applying to all resources in the subnet) and/or individual network interfaces (applying only to that VM NIC); traffic is filtered by the most specific applicable NSG(s). Azure provides default rules that allow intra-VNet and Azure load-balancer traffic and deny all inbound internet traffic; these can be overridden by higher-priority custom rules. Service tags (like `Internet`, `AzureLoadBalancer`, `Storage`) abstract IP ranges maintained by Microsoft, reducing management overhead. NSG flow logs written to storage or Log Analytics enable traffic visibility and forensic analysis.
words.connector: Like a building's access-control list at the entrance and each office door: guards check every visitor against the list and turn away anyone not explicitly permitted.
words.techContext: The team locked the web-tier subnet's NSG to accept only ports 80 and 443 from the internet, and the database-tier NSG to accept 1433 only from the web-tier subnet.
words.exampleSentence: Accidentally leaving port 3389 open in the NSG triggered an Azure Defender alert within minutes, highlighting how quickly bots probe open RDP.

codeExample.code:
# Create an NSG and add an SSH allow rule
az network nsg create --resource-group prod-rg --name web-nsg
az network nsg rule create --resource-group prod-rg --nsg-name web-nsg \
  --name allow-ssh --priority 200 --access Allow \
  --protocol Tcp --destination-port-range 22 --direction Inbound

words.etymology: Descriptive: a 'security group' (firewall ruleset) applied at the 'network' level; mirrors the concept of AWS Security Groups.

words.shortDefinition: A segmented IP address range within a Virtual Network used to group and isolate resources, enabling separate security and routing policies per segment.
words.simpleDefinition: A subnet is a slice of your VNet's IP address space assigned to a specific tier or purpose — web servers, databases, or gateways. Resources in a subnet share NSG and route-table rules. Splitting into subnets lets you enforce different traffic rules between your frontend and backend.
words.longDefinition: An Azure subnet is a named IP address range (CIDR) defined within a Virtual Network's address space, used to segment and organize resources. Each subnet has its own optional Network Security Group (for traffic filtering), User-Defined Route table (to override default routing), and service-endpoint or private-endpoint association for PaaS integration. Azure reserves the first four and last IP addresses in each subnet for internal purposes, so a /29 yields only 3 usable host addresses. Certain services require dedicated subnets: GatewaySubnet for VPN/ExpressRoute gateways, AzureFirewallSubnet for Azure Firewall, and AzureBastionSubnet for Azure Bastion. Subnets enable the principle of least privilege at the network layer — a database subnet can block all internet traffic while the web subnet allows HTTPS inbound — and are the attachment point for service delegation (assigning a subnet exclusively to a PaaS service like Azure Container Apps).
words.connector: Like floors in an office building: each floor has its own badge rules and elevator access, even though they're all inside the same building.
words.techContext: The architecture uses four subnets: web (public-facing), app (internal), data (no internet), and GatewaySubnet for the ExpressRoute connection.
words.exampleSentence: Moving the payment-processing service to its own isolated subnet meant a single NSG rule enforced PCI compliance across all pods in that tier.

codeExample.code:
# Add a subnet to an existing VNet
az network vnet subnet create \
  --resource-group prod-rg \
  --vnet-name prod-vnet \
  --name app-subnet \
  --address-prefix 10.0.2.0/24

words.etymology: From 'sub-' (below, a division of) + 'network'; a standard networking term predating cloud computing.

words.shortDefinition: A routable IPv4 or IPv6 address resource in Azure that can be attached to a VM, load balancer, VPN gateway, or other service to make it reachable from the internet.
words.simpleDefinition: A public IP is a standalone Azure resource representing an internet-routable address. You create one and then attach it to whatever needs internet exposure — a VM, a load balancer, or a VPN gateway. It can be static (never changes) or dynamic (assigned at boot and may change on reallocation).
words.longDefinition: An Azure Public IP Address is a first-class ARM resource that provides an internet-routable IPv4 or IPv6 address for attaching to Azure services. Public IPs have two allocation methods: Static (the address is reserved and never changes, even when the resource is stopped — best for DNS, firewalls, and allowlists) and Dynamic (the address is assigned when the resource starts and released when it is deallocated — suitable for dev environments). SKUs are Basic (legacy, open by default) and Standard (secure by default — inbound blocked unless NSG or load-balancer rule allows; zone-redundant; required for zone-redundant load balancers and VPN Gateways). Standard SKU public IPs incur a small hourly charge even when not associated; reserving a static address for a VPN gateway accounts for a nontrivial cost. Public IP prefixes let you reserve a contiguous block of addresses.
words.connector: Like a published phone number for a business: anyone on the internet can call it, but your internal PBX (NSG/firewall) decides which calls get routed inside.
words.techContext: The internet-facing load balancer has a static Standard SKU public IP so the DNS record and TLS certificate never need updating after failover.
words.exampleSentence: By switching from a dynamic to a static public IP address, we stopped chasing the address every time the NAT gateway was restarted.

codeExample.code:
# Create a static Standard SKU public IP
az network public-ip create \
  --resource-group prod-rg \
  --name prod-pip \
  --sku Standard \
  --allocation-method Static \
  --zone 1 2 3

words.etymology: 'Public' (visible to the internet) + 'IP address' (Internet Protocol address); contrasts with private IPs used within VNets.

words.shortDefinition: A fully managed, intelligent relational database service in the cloud built on the SQL Server engine, with automatic backups, tuning, and high availability included.
words.simpleDefinition: Azure SQL Database is a managed relational database based on SQL Server. Microsoft handles patching, backups, failover, and performance tuning; you just connect and query. It supports standard T-SQL and scales compute and storage independently via the vCore or DTU purchasing models.
words.longDefinition: Azure SQL Database is a Platform-as-a-Service relational database built on the SQL Server engine, delivered as a multi-tenant or single-tenant managed service. It eliminates DBA tasks such as patching, OS maintenance, backup scheduling, and HA configuration — point-in-time restore is available for 1–35 days and geo-redundant backups are enabled by default in most tiers. Purchasing models are DTU (bundled compute/storage/IO for simple workloads) and vCore (separate compute and storage scaling, supports reserved capacity discounts and Azure Hybrid Benefit for SQL Server license portability). Built-in intelligence includes Automatic Tuning (query plan forcing, index recommendations), Intelligent Query Processing from the SQL Server engine, and Advanced Threat Protection. Deployment options are single database (isolated, own resources) or elastic pool (shared compute across many databases for SaaS multi-tenancy). A serverless compute tier auto-pauses and auto-resumes based on activity, charging only for seconds of use.
words.connector: Like hiring a DBA team as a managed service: they run daily backups, tune indexes at night, and flip to the standby server automatically — you just write your queries.
words.techContext: The SaaS application uses an elastic pool of 200 Azure SQL Databases — one per tenant — sharing 800 vCores so lightly used tenants don't each require dedicated provisioned capacity.
words.exampleSentence: After enabling Automatic Tuning on the Azure SQL Database, the slow dashboard query received an index recommendation that the service applied automatically overnight.

codeExample.code:
# Create a logical SQL server and a General Purpose vCore database
az sql server create --resource-group prod-rg --name my-sql-server \
  --admin-user sqladmin --admin-password 'S3cur3P@ss!'
az sql db create --resource-group prod-rg --server my-sql-server \
  --name app-db --edition GeneralPurpose --compute-model Serverless \
  --family Gen5 --capacity 2

words.etymology: 'SQL' = Structured Query Language; 'Azure SQL Database' is the PaaS branded name distinguishing it from SQL Server on VMs or SQL Managed Instance.

words.shortDefinition: A system that grants fine-grained access to Azure resources by assigning roles — containing specific action permissions — to users, groups, or service identities at chosen scopes.
words.simpleDefinition: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) is how you control who can do what in Azure. You assign a built-in or custom role — like 'Reader' or 'Contributor' — to a user or group, scoped to a subscription, resource group, or individual resource. The assignment determines what Azure API actions that identity can perform.
words.longDefinition: Azure Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) is the authorization system built into Azure Resource Manager that controls access to Azure resources. An RBAC assignment has three parts: a security principal (user, group, service principal, or managed identity), a role definition (a named collection of allowed and optionally denied actions expressed as Azure resource-provider operation strings, e.g., `Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/read`), and a scope (management group, subscription, resource group, or individual resource). Assignments are additive and inherited downward — a role at a subscription scope applies to all resource groups within it. Azure provides over 100 built-in roles (Owner, Contributor, Reader, and dozens of service-specific ones); custom roles can combine any subset of permissions. Azure RBAC is enforced by ARM before any action is executed, making it the universal access-control plane. Deny assignments (via blueprints or Azure Policy deny effects) can override RBAC allows.
words.connector: Like a hotel's keycard system: each card (role) is programmed to open specific doors (resources), and the front desk (ARM) checks the card before every door opens.
words.techContext: Developers are assigned the Contributor role scoped to the dev resource group; the same users have only Reader on production, preventing accidental changes.
words.exampleSentence: By assigning the Storage Blob Data Reader role at the storage account scope rather than subscription, least privilege prevented the app from accessing any other resource.

codeExample.code:
# Assign the Contributor role to a user at resource-group scope
az role assignment create \
  --assignee user@contoso.com \
  --role Contributor \
  --scope /subscriptions/<subId>/resourceGroups/dev-rg

words.etymology: RBAC = Role-Based Access Control, a security paradigm from the 1990s academic literature; Azure adopted it as its native authorization model.

words.shortDefinition: A non-human identity created in Microsoft Entra ID that applications, automation scripts, and CI/CD pipelines use to authenticate and call Azure APIs.
words.simpleDefinition: A service principal is like a machine account in Azure: instead of using a human's credentials, your application or pipeline gets its own identity with a client ID and secret (or certificate). You assign it only the permissions it needs, so it can act in Azure on behalf of the application with least privilege.
words.longDefinition: In Microsoft Entra ID, a service principal is the local instantiation of an application registration in a specific tenant — the actual identity object that is assigned roles, consented to permissions, and used for authentication at runtime. Creating an app registration in Entra ID automatically creates a service principal in the same tenant; you can also create service principals directly via the CLI or portal. Service principals authenticate using a client secret, a certificate, or federated credentials (Workload Identity Federation, which allows GitHub Actions or Kubernetes workloads to obtain Entra ID tokens without secrets). They are assigned Azure RBAC roles for resource access and Microsoft Graph / API permissions for Microsoft services. The principle of least privilege requires scoping assignments narrowly. Managed Identities (system- or user-assigned) are the preferred alternative when the workload runs on Azure, eliminating secret management entirely.
words.connector: Like a contractor's company ID badge: it grants access to the building for legitimate business, is scoped to specific areas, and is revoked when the contract ends — independent of any individual employee.
words.techContext: The GitHub Actions workflow uses a service principal with Workload Identity Federation to authenticate to Azure — no client secret stored in repo secrets.
words.exampleSentence: The security review flagged the service principal had Contributor on the entire subscription; it was tightened to Contributor on the target resource group only.

codeExample.code:
# Create a service principal with Contributor on a resource group
az ad sp create-for-rbac \
  --name my-app-sp \
  --role Contributor \
  --scopes /subscriptions/<subId>/resourceGroups/prod-rg

words.etymology: 'Service' (a non-human workload) + 'principal' (a security entity that can be authenticated and authorized); from identity and access management terminology.

words.shortDefinition: A name-value pair you attach to Azure resources for organizing, filtering, and allocating costs across teams, environments, and projects.
words.simpleDefinition: Tags are labels you stick on Azure resources — like `Environment: Production` or `CostCenter: Engineering`. They are free metadata and don't affect functionality. Azure Cost Management uses them to break down bills, and automation scripts use them to find and act on specific resources.
words.longDefinition: An Azure tag is a key-value pair (both strings, max 512 characters for the key and 256 for the value) applied to Azure resource groups and individual resources as metadata. Tags are purely organizational — they do not affect routing, security, or runtime behavior — but they power reporting and automation. Azure Cost Management + Billing can slice spending reports by tag, enabling chargeback and showback across departments, projects, or environments. Azure Policy can enforce required tags (e.g., deny deployment if `CostCenter` is absent) and auto-apply tags via the `Modify` effect. The Azure CLI, Portal, and ARM templates all support tagging at creation or update time. Resources inherit no tags from their resource group by default (unlike some other organizational constructs), so policies are commonly used to propagate tags. Each resource supports up to 50 tag pairs.
words.connector: Like putting a colored sticker on every piece of office equipment to identify which department owns it — handy for the accountants splitting the supply budget.
words.techContext: Azure Policy enforces that every resource must carry the `Owner` and `CostCenter` tags; resources missing these tags are flagged as non-compliant in the Advisor dashboard.
words.exampleSentence: The finance team could instantly see that the ML training workloads — all tagged `Team: DataScience` — accounted for 40% of last month's Azure bill.

codeExample.code:
# Add tags to an existing resource group
az group update \
  --name prod-rg \
  --tags Environment=Production CostCenter=Engineering Owner=platform-team

words.etymology: From 'tag' (a label attached for identification), universally used in cloud platforms and HTML for metadata annotation.

words.shortDefinition: A suite of tools built into Azure for monitoring cloud spending, allocating costs to teams, setting budgets with alerts, and identifying optimization opportunities.
words.simpleDefinition: Azure Cost Management lets you see exactly where your Azure money is going — by service, resource, tag, or subscription — and set budget alerts so you're not surprised at month end. It also surfaces cost-saving recommendations like rightsizing VMs. It is the central place for cloud FinOps work in Azure.
words.longDefinition: Azure Cost Management + Billing is a native Azure capability that provides visibility, governance, and optimization for cloud spend. Core features include cost analysis (interactive charts breaking down spend by subscription, resource group, service, tag, or time), budgets (spending thresholds that trigger email or Action Group alerts at configurable percentages), cost allocation rules for distributing shared costs, exports to Storage for custom BI tooling, and recommendations surfaced from Azure Advisor. It integrates tightly with billing scopes (billing account, billing profile, invoice section, subscription, management group) so finance and engineering teams share the same data. The service is free to use for Azure-native resources; monitoring multi-cloud (AWS/GCP) costs is available via connectors in the paid Microsoft Cost Management offering. Anomaly detection automatically alerts on unexpected spend spikes.
words.connector: Like a corporate expense-management platform: every receipt (resource charge) is categorized, teams see their own totals, and managers set alerts before the card limit is hit.
words.techContext: The platform team creates a budget in Azure Cost Management scoped to each team's resource group with a 90% threshold alert routed to the team's Slack channel via a Logic App.
words.exampleSentence: Azure Cost Management's anomaly detection sent an alert on a Sunday when a runaway CI job spun up 200 VMs and spent $3,000 in two hours.

codeExample.code:
# Create a monthly budget with an 80% alert for a resource group
az consumption budget create \
  --budget-name dev-monthly-budget \
  --amount 500 \
  --time-grain Monthly \
  --resource-group dev-rg \
  --notifications '{"actual_gte_80":{"enabled":true,"operator":"GreaterThanOrEqualTo","threshold":80,"contactEmails":["team@contoso.com"]}}'

words.etymology: 'Cost management' is a standard FinOps term; Microsoft branded the Azure capability 'Azure Cost Management + Billing' when it merged the cost and billing portals.

words.shortDefinition: A free web tool on the Azure website that lets you configure Azure services and get an estimated monthly cost before committing to any deployment.
words.simpleDefinition: The Azure Pricing Calculator is a website where you pick the services you plan to use — VM sizes, storage tiers, bandwidth, databases — and it generates a cost estimate. You can share or export the estimate for budget approval. It is the first step when scoping the cost of an Azure architecture.
words.longDefinition: The Azure Pricing Calculator (available at azure.microsoft.com/pricing/calculator) is a free, publicly accessible web tool for estimating Azure expenditure. Users add products to a scenario, configure parameters (region, tier, quantity, reservation term, license type), and the calculator totals a monthly estimate. Estimates can be saved, shared via URL, or exported to Excel for budget submissions. The calculator reflects list pricing; it does not account for enterprise-agreement discounts, Azure Hybrid Benefit, or reserved-instance discounts unless configured. It complements the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) Calculator, which estimates savings from migrating on-premises workloads to Azure. Estimates are approximations — actual bills depend on measured usage, egress patterns, and support plan charges — making the calculator most useful for order-of-magnitude sizing rather than precise forecasting.
words.connector: Like an online configurator for a new car: you pick options, see the sticker price, and know roughly what to budget — the final invoice still depends on taxes and dealer fees.
words.techContext: Before the architecture review, the cloud architect shared an Azure Pricing Calculator link showing the estimated $4,200/month for the proposed AKS cluster and SQL Database configuration.
words.exampleSentence: The product manager was surprised to see how much cheaper switching from Premium SSD to Standard SSD was in the Azure Pricing Calculator — enough to justify the architecture change.

codeExample.code:
# Look up the retail price for a specific VM SKU via the Price API
curl -s 'https://prices.azure.com/api/retail/prices?api-version=2023-01-01-preview&$filter=armRegionName eq '"'"'eastus'"'"' and skuName eq '"'"'D2s v5'"'"'' | python3 -m json.tool | grep retailPrice

words.etymology: Descriptive: a 'calculator' (a tool that computes) for Azure 'pricing' (the cost schedule).

words.shortDefinition: A starter offer providing new Azure users with 12 months of popular services free, a $200 credit for 30 days, and access to over 55 always-free services.
words.simpleDefinition: The Azure free account is how most developers first try Azure: you get $200 in credits to spend on any service in the first 30 days, 12 months of specific services at no charge, and a permanent set of always-free services with usage limits. After the trial period, you can convert to pay-as-you-go.
words.longDefinition: Azure's free account tier is a welcome offer for new customers that includes three distinct layers: a $200 USD credit valid for 30 days (usable on any Azure service, with a monthly cap on some high-cost services like GPU VMs); 12-month free access to a specific set of popular services up to defined usage limits (e.g., 750 hours of B1s Linux VMs, 5 GB of Blob Storage, a free Azure SQL Database); and more than 55 always-free products with perpetual usage quotas (e.g., Azure Functions up to 1 million executions/month, Azure Static Web Apps, Azure DevOps for up to 5 users). The account requires a credit card for identity verification but is not charged unless you explicitly upgrade and exceed the free limits. It is designed to let individuals and startups learn, prototype, and build proof-of-concepts without upfront cost.
words.connector: Like a gym's free trial pass: 30 days of full access to explore everything, plus a few machines you can use indefinitely after the trial, so you keep coming back.
words.techContext: The startup used an Azure free account to build and demo their MVP — the $200 credit covered the AKS cluster and SQL Database prototyping — before signing an enterprise agreement.
words.exampleSentence: She created an Azure free account to complete the certification labs without spending any money, using the always-free services tier for her sample app.

codeExample.code:
# Check remaining free-tier quota for a subscription (spending)
az consumption usage list \
  --start-date 2026-06-01 --end-date 2026-06-14 \
  --query '[].{Service:consumedService,Cost:pretaxCost}' \
  --output table

words.etymology: 'Free account' is a marketing term describing the no-cost trial tier; Azure's free offer was formalized and expanded around 2017.

words.shortDefinition: A personalized cloud consultant built into Azure that analyzes your deployed resources and provides actionable recommendations across cost, security, reliability, performance, and operational excellence.
words.simpleDefinition: Azure Advisor is a built-in tool that reviews your Azure resources and tells you what to improve — unused VMs to delete, security gaps to fix, or settings to change for better reliability. Recommendations are prioritized (High/Medium/Low) and many can be applied with one click. It is like a free architectural review that runs continuously.
words.longDefinition: Azure Advisor is an Azure-native, free recommendation engine that continuously analyzes the configuration and usage of your Azure resources against a library of best-practice rules across five pillars: Cost (rightsizing, shutting down idle resources, reserved-instance opportunities), Security (aligned with Microsoft Defender for Cloud recommendations, missing MFA, exposed management ports), Reliability (availability set usage, geo-redundant storage, backup enablement), Performance (SQL Database advisor, app service performance improvements, premium cache sizing), and Operational Excellence (deprecated APIs, resource health, subscription limits). Recommendations include impact assessment, estimated savings, and one-click or scripted remediation. Advisor integrates with Azure Policy to suppress known false positives, and its findings feed the Azure Secure Score for security posture tracking. Recommendations are scoped to a subscription or management group and exportable via the REST API.
words.connector: Like a diligent building inspector who walks through your property every day, posts a punch list on the door, and sometimes offers to fix the issue on the spot.
words.techContext: Advisor flagged three underutilized VMs averaging 3% CPU over 14 days and estimated $1,200/month in savings if they were resized to B-series burstable instances.
words.exampleSentence: The quarterly FinOps review starts by exporting the Azure Advisor cost recommendations — last quarter those tips saved the team $8,000 in idle resource charges.

codeExample.code:
# List high-impact cost recommendations from Advisor
az advisor recommendation list \
  --category Cost \
  --query "[?impact=='High'].{Resource:resourceMetadata.resourceId,Recommendation:shortDescription.solution}" \
  --output table

words.etymology: From 'advisor' (one who gives counsel); Microsoft chose the term to position the service as a personalized recommendation engine rather than a passive monitoring tool.

words.shortDefinition: A VM grouping that spreads instances across multiple fault domains and update domains within a single data center to protect against hardware failures and planned maintenance downtime.
words.simpleDefinition: An availability set tells Azure to place your VMs on different physical hardware racks (fault domains) and to patch them in waves (update domains). This way, a power strip failure or a planned OS update never takes down all your VMs at once. It is the older HA mechanism for VMs, predating Availability Zones.
words.longDefinition: An Azure Availability Set is a logical grouping of Virtual Machines that provides two protection mechanisms within a single data center (and therefore a single Availability Zone). Fault Domains (FDs, max 3) represent separate racks with independent power and network switches; VMs spread across FDs avoid a correlated hardware failure taking all instances offline. Update Domains (UDs, max 20) are logical groups that Azure updates one at a time during planned maintenance; VMs in different UDs ensure at least some instances remain available during host patching. Together, FDs and UDs give a 99.95% VM SLA (vs. 99.9% for a single VM). Availability Sets are appropriate for same-region HA without the complexity of multi-zone deployment, but they do not protect against data-center (AZ)-level failures the way Availability Zones do. They are free — you pay only for the VMs inside.
words.connector: Like distributing your restaurant's waitstaff across different sections and different shift rotations: a section's power failure or a shift's sick leave never leaves all tables unattended.
words.techContext: The legacy application can't be refactored to span zones, so the two web VMs are placed in an availability set across two fault domains to satisfy the 99.95% SLA requirement.
words.exampleSentence: When Azure performed planned maintenance on one update domain, the load balancer continued routing traffic to VMs in the other update domains — users saw no downtime.

codeExample.code:
# Create an availability set with 3 fault domains and 5 update domains
az vm availability-set create \
  --resource-group prod-rg \
  --name web-avset \
  --platform-fault-domain-count 3 \
  --platform-update-domain-count 5

words.etymology: 'Availability set' is a descriptive Microsoft term: a 'set' of resources grouped for high 'availability'; introduced in early Azure IaaS offerings.
